Course Overview

HS U.S. History: Reconstruction to Present is a 10th grade study of American history from Reconstruction through World War I. Scholars examine the political settlement after the Civil War, the Gilded Age’s industrial transformation, the labor movement and urbanization, Progressive Era reforms, American imperial expansion, and U.S. entry into World War I, using primary sources, including Theodore Roosevelt’s extensive writings, and virtual reality to engage with the key people and events of this era.

What Scholars Will Learn to Do

  • Analyze the political and social consequences of Reconstruction, including the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments.
  • Analyze the causes and consequences of American imperial expansion and the Spanish-American War.
  • Examine the causes and effects of the Second Industrial Revolution, including big business, railroads, and labor movements.
  • Examine the domestic and international causes of U.S. involvement in World War I.
  • Evaluate Gilded Age social and political reforms and the rise of muckraking journalism.
  • Interpret primary source documents, including political speeches, legislation, and investigative journalism.
  • Trace Progressive Era reforms in politics, economics, housing, and conservation.

Live (Synchronous) Learning

In the Live section you join scheduled class meetings on Optima’s VR campus, where your teacher leads instruction in real time and you learn alongside classmates. The readings, assignments, and projects are the same as the On-Demand course; what differs is the pacing · a Live section moves through the material together on the class schedule rather than at each scholar’s own pace, and class time is also used for discussion, questions, and guided practice.

Attendance is measured by presence and participation. You are expected to attend the scheduled live sessions, on time and ready to take part. If you must miss a class, notify the school in advance; your teacher will let you know how to make up the work and any material you missed. As in every Optima course, completing your work means a sincere attempt · real effort on real work · and assignments still open and close with each quarter.

You meet regularly with a teacher. The class gathers throughout the week in VR and on Microsoft Teams for live instruction and discussion.

This course is also offered as an On-Demand (asynchronous) section that scholars pace themselves. If that is the section you are enrolled in, use the On-Demand syllabus instead of this one.

Using AI in This Course

Optima’s AI policy does not ask whether a scholar used AI. It asks whether AI was used honestly, skillfully, and in a way that genuinely built your own thinking. AI may support your work, but it may not do the reasoning an assignment asks of you.

Which AI tools you may use

  • Every scholar. Any AI used for this course is school-controlled: tools built into Canvas assignments and into Optima’s VR platform, set up to ask you questions and prompt your thinking rather than hand you answers. No assignment in this course requires a personal AI account.
  • Scholars under 14. Your teacher may not ask, suggest, or require that you use an AI tool outside those school-controlled platforms. Your AI work for this course happens in Canvas and in VR.
  • Scholars 14 and older. Whether you use an outside AI tool for schoolwork is your family’s decision, not the school’s. It requires written parent or guardian permission on file with your teacher, and your parent or guardian selects the tool, sets up the account, monitors it, and stays responsible for it. Optima does not provide, endorse, or manage personal AI accounts. Your teacher’s part is to judge whether the AI was used well.

What is expected when you use AI

  • Document it. Record the tool, the prompt you gave it, and the date. Using AI is not plagiarism. Turning in AI-generated work as entirely your own thought, with no documentation, is.
  • Verify it. AI states wrong things confidently, and you are responsible for every claim you submit, so check it against a credible source before it goes into your work. Verification is one of the skills this course grades.
  • Sound like yourself. Your work should read the way you write and speak in the rest of the course, take a real position rather than hedging, and be something you can explain on the spot, on camera or in VR, when your teacher asks a follow-up question you did not expect.
  • Keep the process, not just the product. Prompt logs, drafts, revision notes, and VR recordings are gradeable evidence of your thinking. When an assignment asks for them, they count toward your grade.

Some assignments limit or exclude AI so that you build the underlying skill yourself, and the assignment page will say so. The reason is practical: you cannot judge whether an AI’s answer is any good unless you can do the work without it.

Learning in Virtual Reality

Optima is a virtual-reality school. Alongside your Canvas coursework, you will join immersive sessions on Optima’s VR campus, where you meet teachers and fellow scholars, take part in live activities, and explore places and ideas you could not visit in an ordinary classroom. Keep your headset charged and ready for any scheduled VR sessions, and treat the VR campus with the same courtesy and seriousness you would a physical one. If you ever cannot get into VR for a session, tell your teacher · there is an alternative way to take part so you do not fall behind.

Being an Optima Scholar

Optima’s mission is an excellent, virtue-centered education, and virtue is at the center of this course as much as any other. Every scholar is expected to practice the seven virtues that shape life at Optima · courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. In practice that means: do your own honest work; treat everyone you meet in, through, or because of this course with respect, in writing, in discussion, and in VR; engage actively rather than passively; come to office hours to get help, meet other scholars, and get to know your teacher; and take responsibility for your own work and progress. You belong to a house and a community of scholars, not only to a course.

What You Need & Staying Connected

  • A computer with reliable internet and access to Canvas.
  • A VR headset, charged and ready for scheduled immersive sessions.
  • Microsoft 365 (Word, PowerPoint) with OneDrive, for documents you create and submit.
  • A notebook or binder, and pens or pencils, for reading notes and primary source work.

Staying connected. Updates about this course are posted on the course’s Canvas page; school-wide updates are posted in your Homeroom Canvas course. Check both regularly. Your teacher holds office hours and is glad to help with the material, to meet you, or to talk through your plans · come by, or reach out any time by email.

pages.html:
Course Overview

Course Map: The 18-Week Sequence

U.S. History: Reconstruction to Present. Quarter 1 covers Weeks 1 to 9; Quarter 2 covers Weeks 10 to 18.

This map shows the whole path of the course at a glance. You will begin with the political settlement that followed the Civil War, move through the Gilded Age and the rise of industry, cities, and mass culture, study the reform movements and religious currents that answered them, follow the United States as it becomes an empire abroad, and finish with the outbreak of World War I and America's entry into it. Every week has a topic, and every week has one or two primary sources: real documents written by the people who lived through these events.

How a normal week runs
  • Monday: Lesson 1, then the Reading Quiz.
  • Tuesday: Primary Source 1, then Critical Questions. In some weeks a required VR activity takes this place instead.
  • Wednesday: Lesson 2.
  • Thursday: Primary Source 2, then the Primary Source Exercise.
  • Friday: the Week Wrap-Up, including a short checklist so you can confirm everything is submitted.

Weeks 5 and 6 read a single primary source rather than two, so those weeks have one source day instead of two.

Quarter 1: Weeks 1 to 9

Reconstruction through the American empire.

Week Topic Primary Sources
1 Reconstruction: the political settlement after the Civil War and the new constitutions written in the South. Discussion: the Grant presidency. The 14th Amendment
The Reconstruction Act of 1867
2 The West and agrarian America: the Homestead Act, settlement of the Great Plains, the Indian wars and reservations, and the cattle drives. Discussion: the Grange movement and agrarian populism. Theodore Roosevelt, Ranch Life and the Hunting Trail (excerpt)
Marcus Reno, account of the Battle of the Little Bighorn
3 The Gilded Age: the rise of heavy industry. Discussion: railroads transform America, and Vanderbilt. Theodore Judah, A Practical Plan for Building the Pacific Railroad
Mark Twain, Roughing It
4 Big business consolidation: the industrialists and the rise of the managerial and working classes. Discussion: Rockefeller and the Standard Oil trust. Theodore Roosevelt on the trusts (autobiography excerpt)
Andrew Carnegie, The Gospel of Wealth
5 Urbanization and the growth of America's great cities. Discussion: Andrew Carnegie and Pittsburgh, the steel city. Herbert Casson, The Romance of Steel
(one source this week)
6 Transformative inventions and the beginning of mass culture and consumer society. Discussion: Thomas Edison and the light bulb. Thomas Edison, papers and correspondence
(one source this week)
7 Backlash against the Gilded Age: robber barons, muckrakers, unions, and strikes. Discussion: Ida Tarbell and investigative journalism. Theodore Roosevelt, message to Congress on the 1902 coal strike arbitration
Upton Sinclair, The Jungle
8 Religion and culture: revivalism, care for the urban poor, foreign missions, and the Social Gospel. Discussion: Protestantism mobilized, temperance and the American missionary movement. Frances Willard, Glimpses of Fifty Years
Walter Rauschenbusch on the Social Gospel
9 American empire: the Spanish-American War and the acquisition of Hawaii and the Philippines. Discussion: Joseph Pulitzer and yellow journalism. Theodore Roosevelt, The Rough Riders
Theodore Roosevelt, The Strenuous Life

Quarter 2: Weeks 10 to 18

The new immigration through America's entry into World War I.

Week Topic Primary Sources
10 The new immigration: southern and eastern Europe come to America's cities. Discussion: Bensonhurst, Brooklyn's Little Italy. Theodore Roosevelt on the Americanization of immigrants

pages.title: M365 Setup & File Organization Guide
pages.html:
There are a few things worth setting up once, at the start, so that turning in written work later is simple. This page stays available all year. Come back to it whenever you need it, especially before your first Critical Questions or Primary Source Exercise submission.

Signing in to Microsoft 365

Your school gives you a Microsoft 365 account. It is the one you use for schoolwork.

  1. Go to office.com.
  2. Sign in with your school Microsoft account, not a personal one. Your school account is the one with your school email address.
  3. Once you are signed in, you can open Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and OneDrive from that same page.

Everything you save while signed in to your school account is saved to your school OneDrive, where you and your teacher can both find it.

Your OneDrive folder for this course

Keep your schoolwork organized the way you would keep a binder organized: one folder per subject, one folder inside it per course. By this grade band you maintain this structure yourself.

For this course, your folder path is:

Optima > History > USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27

If those folders do not exist yet, make them in OneDrive: New, then Folder, named Optima; inside it, History; inside that, USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27.

Naming your files

Every file you turn in uses the same naming pattern:

LastName_FirstName_AssignmentName_CourseCode

The course code for this course is HIS10. So a student named Jane Smith, turning in one week's Critical Questions, would name her file:

Smith_Jane_14thAmendmentCriticalQ_HIS10

A few rules that go with it:

  • Use underscores, not spaces.
  • If a specific assignment asks for drafts, the version you actually turn in ends in _Final, and earlier drafts end in _Draft1, _Draft2, and so on. Never delete an earlier draft or save over it.
  • Most weeks in this course, the file you are naming is that week's Critical Questions or Primary Source Exercise, submitted as a single Word document with no draft required, so the plain LastName_FirstName_AssignmentName_HIS10 pattern above is what you will use most often.

Which program to use

What you are making What to open
Critical Questions, a Primary Source Exercise, or any other written responseWord
A slide presentation, if a specific assignment asks for onePowerPoint
A table of data or numbers, if a specific assignment asks for oneExcel

Almost every written assignment in this course is a Word document. VR activities usually ask you to submit a recording link and a screenshot directly into Canvas instead, not a separate file.

Turning your work in through Canvas

  1. Finish your document in Word and make sure it is saved in your USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27 folder.
  2. Open the assignment in Canvas and click Submit Assignment.
  3. Choose the OneDrive tab if you see one, then pick your file. If you do not see a OneDrive tab, choose File Upload instead.
  4. Click Submit, then check that Canvas shows your file name back to you. If it does not, the file did not go through.

That last step matters. A submission you did not confirm is the most common way good work ends up ungraded.

One thing worth knowing about OneDrive

OneDrive saves as you type, and it keeps a history of your changes. If you delete a paragraph and want it back an hour later, open File, then Info, then Version History.

This is a real habit worth building now: it means your work is never one mistake away from being lost.

If you joined this course partway through the semester

Welcome. Do these four things and you will be caught up on the setup side:

  1. Check that you can sign in at office.com with your school account. If you cannot, message your teacher.
  2. Make your Optima > History > USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27 folder if it is not already there.
  3. Read the file naming rule above and bookmark this page.
  4. Ask your teacher whether any earlier week's Critical Questions or Primary Source Exercise still needs to be turned in.

Where to get help

Message your teacher through Canvas. If you want to practice a Word skill on your own, Microsoft keeps short beginner guides at support.microsoft.com.

pages.title: 0.4 Teacher's Guide to This Course
pages.html:
Facilitator Reference

Teacher's Guide to This Course

U.S. History: Reconstruction to Present, Grade 10. Master copy, shared across all sections.

This page explains how the course is built, so that every facilitator teaching a section is working from the same content, the same sequence, and the same expectations. It is a master copy: it is deliberately not personalized to any one teacher, term, or set of office hours. Add your own contact information and dates in your section's announcements and syllabus, not here.

The built course covers Weeks 1 to 18, Reconstruction through the United States' entry into World War I. Quarter 1 is Weeks 1 to 9; Quarter 2 is Weeks 10 to 18. The course is fully asynchronous and exists in a Live variant and an On-Demand variant. Where the two differ, keep them separate: link the On-Demand assessment to the On-Demand lesson and the Live assessment to the Live lesson. Do not cross-wire them.

How each week is organized

Every week follows the same five-day rhythm, matching the design document's sample week for this course:

  • Monday: the Week Module Map (ungraded orientation), then Lesson 1 (roughly 1,000 to 1,300 words of original instructional prose at a 9th-grade reading level), paired with an auto-graded Reading Quiz.
  • Tuesday: Primary Source 1 (a real historical excerpt, roughly 500 to 2,000 words), paired with Critical Questions. In the eight weeks where a VR activity is the week's principal assignment (Weeks 2, 3, 7, 9, 12, 15, 16, and 18), the required VR activity takes this slot instead.
  • Wednesday: Lesson 2. On weeks without a principal VR activity, an optional midweek VR activity sits here.
  • Thursday: Primary Source 2, paired with the Primary Source Exercise (open-ended, reasoning-quality graded).
  • Friday: the Week Wrap-Up page and its submissions checklist, paired with an optional capstone gallery VR activity.

Two weeks depart from this shape by design, not by oversight. Weeks 5 and 6 carry a single primary source rather than two, exactly as the course map specifies. Do not add a second source to either week.

Each Canvas module opens with a short Module Check-In survey and closes with a Module Reflection survey. These capture the week's essential question before and after the content, a confidence rating, and a place for students to name what is still unclear. They are ungraded and they are the fastest way to see, at a glance, where a cohort is struggling.

Where the content actually lives

Lessons, primary sources, and wrap-up pages are not authored in Canvas. Each one is a standalone hosted web page, embedded into its Canvas page inside an iframe. That is what makes the hover definitions, the audio pronunciation, and the interactive widgets work; Canvas strips the code that powers them if you paste the content in directly.

The practical consequence: do not edit lesson text in the Canvas rich content editor. Your change will look correct until the next deployment overwrites it. Content corrections start in the course build source and flow outward to both the hosted pages and Canvas. Report an error to the course lead rather than patching it in place.

Everything that is graded or teacher-reviewed is Canvas-native: quizzes, assignments, discussions, rubrics, and the module check-in and reflection surveys. That split is deliberate. Canvas owns the gradebook and the analytics; the hosted pages own the reading experience.

The assessment types

Item What it is, and what it costs you
Reading Quiz Weekly, multiple choice, five to eight questions, auto-graded in Canvas. Questions are written to require inference from the lesson, not fact lookup. No grading time.
Critical Questions Weekly, exactly four open-ended questions on Primary Source 1, worth 10 points. Questions rotate among counterfactual, causal, and conceptual types. The category is never named to students; do not name it in feedback either. Deep-feedback item: graded on the quality of the reasoning, not on whether a fact was retrieved.
Primary Source Exercise Weekly, exactly four open-ended questions on Primary Source 2, worth 10 points. Same standard as Critical Questions. Week 9's exercise carries a dedicated question on the reliability of the source itself.
VR activities Two per week, all 18 weeks, written to be completed solo at home with a headset. In Weeks 2, 3, 7, 9, 12, 15, 16, and 18 one of them is the week's required graded deliverable, worth 10 points. In every other week both are optional and ungraded, at your discretion. Many of them build toward that quarter's capstone.
Week Wrap-Up Friday scaffolding: a short review and a submissions checklist. Ungraded.

The two open-ended weekly items are the ones that carry real grading weight and real teacher time. If you have to triage in a heavy week, triage the written comments, not the score: a brief, specific note on one weak paragraph is worth more to a student than three sentences of general praise.

The two quarter capstones

Each quarter ends with a capstone essay worth 100 points, submitted through its own Canvas module rather than folded into a weekly module:

  • Quarter 1 Capstone: A Nation Transformed, 1865 to 1898, submitted at the end of Week 9.
  • Quarter 2 Capstone: Idealism and Its Limits, 1898 to 1919, introduced at the start of Week 17 and submitted at the end of Week 18.

Both use the same four-criterion rubric, 25 points each, so a student who reads the Quarter 1 feedback carefully knows exactly what Quarter 2 will ask of them:

Criterion What earns the points
Understanding of the material Accurately represents what the assigned lessons and primary sources actually say; no significant factual errors.
Quality of reasoning The answer to the essential question follows from the evidence presented, engages counterarguments, and reasons about causation rather than listing facts.
Clarity and precision of expression Organized around a clear thesis; each paragraph does identifiable work; language is precise rather than vague.
Intellectual honesty Acknowledges genuine complexity or uncertainty where it exists rather than overstating confidence; does not force evidence to fit a predetermined conclusion.

Exams

Four exam instruments are built into the course, all multiple choice with four options, all Canvas-native and auto-graded, and none of them requiring a hosted page:

  • Quarter 1 Exam, 27 items, covering Weeks 1 to 9 only.
  • Quarter 2 Exam, 27 items, covering Weeks 10 to 18 only. It is not cumulative.
  • Semester Final Exam, 36 items, two per week across all 18 weeks, including several questions that deliberately ask students to connect material across the two quarters.
  • EOC Practice Exam (Optional), 24 items, carrying no grade weight. It is labeled on its face as partial in scope, because it can only test what Weeks 1 to 18 actually taught. Present it to students that way as well; it is practice with the question format and the reasoning, not a full dry run.

Appendix activities

A separate Appendix module holds five activities that sit outside the weekly rhythm. Each names the week after which it can be assigned. Four are 10-point assignments and one is an optional ungraded VR enrichment activity:

  • A1. Yellow Journalism and the Reliability of Sources (10 points, assign after Week 9). Students weigh three conflicting accounts of a famous quotation and judge which can be trusted.
  • A2. Mapping the Closing Frontier (VR, optional, ungraded enrichment).
  • A3. Two Immigrant Experiences: Europe and Asia (10 points).
  • A4. Florida in the Gilded Age and the Spanish-American War (10 points).
  • A5. A Diverse Army: Who Fought and Who Stayed Home in World War I (10 points).

Interactive widgets and glossaries

Several lessons contain a working interactive element: a map, a comparison, a build-a-trust simulation, a before-and-after view of a tenement. These are real, hosted, and embedded, not design sketches. Every one includes a Reset control, so a student who gets tangled can start over without reloading the page. If a widget fails to load for a student, the usual cause is a blocked iframe in their browser rather than a broken activity.

Every lesson opens with a single combined Glossary of Subject Vocabulary box holding that lesson's new terms in alphabetical order, each with a plain definition, a pronunciation respelling, and an audio button. In the body text, a glossed term is bold and hover-defined at its first appearance in that lesson. A term appears in the glossary box in the lesson where it first appears in the course and in the next lesson, then drops out, so the boxes stay short.

Two things to hold to

  • Keep benchmark codes off student-facing pages. Standards documentation for this course is teacher-facing and lives in the build materials and the facilitator master copy, not in anything a student opens. If you find a code in a student-facing quiz, assignment, or page, report it as a defect.
  • Do not name the method to students. Question types, tier labels, and pedagogical categories are for your planning. To the student, a counterfactual question is simply a hard, interesting question, and that is how it should read.

Grading weights are set by the course lead, not by this page. The point values above (10 points for each weekly open-ended item, 100 for each capstone) are fixed in the build. How the assignment groups are weighted against one another, and where the exams and capstones sit in the overall grade, is a policy decision made at the course level. Check your section's syllabus and gradebook setup before telling a student what an item is worth as a percentage.

Questions or corrections go to the course lead so the fix lands in the build source and reaches every section, not just yours.

assignments.title: 1.5 Critical Questions: The 14th Amendment
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the 14th Amendment) and this week's lessons.

Directions: Answer each question in complete sentences, grounding your reasoning in the primary source and this week's lessons. These questions do not have a single correct answer; the quality of your reasoning matters as much as your conclusion.

  1. Section 1 declares that anyone born in the United States is a citizen. Given that the Supreme Court had ruled in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) that Black Americans could never be citizens, what specific problem is this sentence designed to solve, and how does its wording directly overturn that ruling?

  2. This section restrains the actions of states specifically ("No State shall..."), even though the Bill of Rights already restrained the federal government. Why would Congress in 1866 have felt it necessary to bind state governments by a new constitutional amendment rather than relying on the existing Bill of Rights?

  3. Section 2 does not directly guarantee Black men the right to vote. It only threatens a state with reduced representation if it denies that right. Suppose Congress had instead written Section 2 as a direct national mandate guaranteeing Black male suffrage, the approach the 15th Amendment actually took two years later, rather than this indirect financial penalty. Would a Fourteenth Amendment written that way in 1866 likely have survived ratification by the three-fourths of states then required? Why or why not?

  4. Section 3 allows Congress to remove the office-holding disqualification by a two-thirds vote of both houses. What does the existence of this escape clause suggest about how Congress expected its relationship with former Confederates to change over time?

M365 Skill Step (full treatment, Module 1): Type your answers in a new Word document, not directly into the Canvas text box. Open Word from your school Microsoft 365 account, name the file LastName_FirstName_14thAmendmentCriticalQ_HIS10, save it to your Optima → History → USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27 OneDrive folder, and submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab. See the pinned M365 Setup & File Organization Guide if you need a refresher.

assignments.title: 1.7 VR Activity 1: Congress Divided (optional)
assignments.html:
What you're doing: Reconstruction was decided by an argument, not just an army. You'll examine the two competing cases, Johnson's and the Radical Republicans', and build your own comparison of what each side thought Reconstruction was for.

How to join: Join the VR session using the code posted in Canvas. Setting: "1866 Congress Chamber." You'll start at the center aisle facing the rostrum.

  1. Walk to the two lecterns on either side of the chamber floor. Each holds a reference image with a key quotation: one from Johnson's veto of the Freedmen's Bureau bill, one from Thaddeus Stevens's floor speech on Reconstruction.
  2. Read both placards carefully.
  3. Place a sticky note beneath the position you find more persuasive, explaining your reasoning in two to three sentences.
  4. At the whiteboard at the front of the chamber, sketch or type a two-column comparison: what each side believed the true purpose of Reconstruction should be.
  5. Record a 60 to 90 second recording of yourself explaining your comparison to the whiteboard.

What to submit: your recording link and a screenshot of your sticky note.

Time: about 20 minutes.

This activity is not scored for correctness. It is offered at the teacher's discretion to deepen this week's material.

assignments.title: 1.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Reconstruction Act of 1867
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Reconstruction Act of 1867).

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. What specific action taken by Southern state legislatures directly caused Congress to escalate from Johnson's lenient plan to the military districts described in this Act?

  2. Suppose Congress had allowed the Southern states back into the Union immediately after ratifying only the 13th Amendment, without the military districts, new constitutions, or Black male suffrage this Act required. Would Black civil rights in the South likely have fared better, worse, or about the same as they did under actual Reconstruction? Defend your answer with reference to the Black Codes described in Monday's lesson.

  3. Section 6 declares the existing state governments in the South "provisional only... subject to the paramount authority of the United States." What does this reveal about how Congress understood the constitutional status of the former Confederate states: were they still states in the full sense, conquered territories, or something in between? Defend your answer using the text.

  4. Section 3 gives military commanders the duty to "suppress insurrection, disorder, and violence" and, per later sections, to convene military tribunals when they judge civil courts inadequate. What tension does this create with the ordinary constitutional principle of civilian control and trial by jury, and why might Congress have accepted that tension in 1867?

assignments.title: 2.9 Primary Source Exercise: Reno's Report on the Little Bighorn
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, Major Marcus Reno's official report on the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Reno claims that continuing his initial charge against the village "would have been suicide." What specifically about the situation he describes (numbers, terrain, support) led him to break off and retreat to the bluffs instead of pressing forward?

  2. Reno argues that if the whole regiment had stayed together rather than splitting into three columns (his own, Custer's, and Benteen's), "it would have shared the fate of the five companies under Custer." Do you find this argument persuasive, or could a unified regiment plausibly have fought off the same force that destroyed Custer's battalion? Defend your answer.

  3. This report was written by an officer whose own conduct during the battle was later publicly questioned and investigated. Does knowing that change how you should read his account of why the retreat was necessary? What does this suggest about evaluating primary sources for authorial bias?

  4. This week frames Plains Indian power as a genuine military obstacle to American settlement, not merely a footnote before an inevitable American victory. How does Reno's report, written from inside the losing side of this particular battle, support or complicate that framing?

assignments.title: 3.9 Primary Source Exercise: Twain's Pony Express
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, Mark Twain's Roughing It.

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Twain wrote Roughing It a decade after his stagecoach journey west, for a national reading audience. Given that the Pony Express he describes had already been replaced by the transcontinental telegraph and, soon after, the railroad itself, what larger idea about the West might Twain be using this fleeting, almost dreamlike image to express?

  2. The Pony Express operated for less than two years (1860 to 1861) before it was shut down. Based on this week's lesson about railroads and the coming of the transcontinental telegraph, what specifically made the Pony Express obsolete so quickly?

  3. Suppose the transcontinental railroad had been finished in 1859 instead of 1869. Would the Pony Express, as Twain describes it, have existed at all? Why or why not?

  4. Twain's language ("winging away like a belated fragment of a storm") is closer to poetry than to a factual report. Does this make the passage less useful as a historical source about the Pony Express, or does it capture something a plain factual account would miss? Defend your answer.

assignments.title: 4.5 Critical Questions: Roosevelt on the Trusts
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Roosevelt's Second Annual Message to Congress, 1902) and this week's lessons.

Directions: Answer each question in complete sentences, grounding your reasoning in the primary source and this week's lessons.

  1. Roosevelt insists the line he draws is "on conduct, not upon wealth." Based on Monday's lesson, what specific kind of "conduct" by trusts would most likely have concerned him: the mere fact of consolidation itself, or a more particular set of practices? Explain using the difference between Vanderbilt's and Gould's methods from Week 3.

  2. Why might a president who says "we draw the line against misconduct, not against wealth" nonetheless pursue major antitrust lawsuits, as Roosevelt did against Northern Securities the same year as this message? Is there a contradiction here, or a consistent principle?

  3. Suppose Roosevelt had instead drawn his line at wealth itself, proposing to break up any corporation above a certain size regardless of how it behaved. Given what you know of Vanderbilt's and Gould's very different methods from Week 3, would a size-based standard have caught the trusts everyone agreed were harmful without also punishing genuinely well-run consolidations? Defend your answer.

  4. Roosevelt calls a capitalist who wins money through "some great industrial feat" a "well-doer, not a wrong-doer." How does this square, or fail to square, with the Classical Republican framework's insistence that virtue is judged by whether an activity serves the common good, not merely by whether it is legal?

M365 Reminder. Type your answers in Word, save to your Optima → History → USHistoryReconPresent_2026-27 folder using the naming rule, and submit via the Canvas OneDrive tab.

assignments.title: 4.9 Primary Source Exercise: Carnegie's Gospel of Wealth
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (Andrew Carnegie, The Gospel of Wealth).

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Carnegie says the wealthy man should treat his surplus as "trust funds... administered" for the community's benefit, while otherwise leaving "the laws of accumulation... free." What economic and political philosophy is Carnegie defending by insisting that redistribution should be voluntary and personal rather than achieved through law or taxation?

  2. Carnegie built his own fortune in steel using many of the same efficiency-driven consolidation methods Rockefeller used in oil. What in Carnegie's own career might explain why he came to believe surplus wealth carried a moral duty of administration, rather than simply a right of ownership?

  3. Suppose every Gilded Age industrialist had sincerely followed Carnegie's gospel and given away the bulk of their fortunes as he recommends. Would this have addressed the underlying economic grievances of industrial wage earners described in Monday's lesson, or only their symptoms? Defend your answer.

  4. Carnegie calls the millionaire "a trustee for the poor" who administers wealth "far better than [the community] could or would have done for itself." What assumption about the poor's own judgment is built into this claim, and is it a fair one?

assignments.title: 5.8 Primary Source Exercise: Casson on Carnegie
assignments.html:
Covers: the primary source, Herbert N. Casson's The Romance of Steel.

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. What specific business strategy, described in Tuesday's lesson, explains how Carnegie Steel could out-produce and out-price competitors even without the secret rebate schemes Rockefeller used?

  2. Suppose Carnegie had instead pursued horizontal integration, like Rockefeller, buying out competing steel mills rather than acquiring mines, ships, and railroads. Would Carnegie Steel likely have achieved the same cost advantage? Why or why not?

  3. Casson's phrase "the faculty of attracting the attention of the great and the rich" credits Carnegie's rise partly to a personal, almost intangible quality rather than to a specific business decision. Does this kind of explanation belong in a rigorous historical account, or is it too vague to count as historical evidence? Defend your answer.

  4. Casson describes Carnegie directing "the battle from a near-by hill" while trusting subordinates like Henry Clay Frick to run daily operations. Tuesday's lesson notes that historians still debate how much responsibility Carnegie bears for what Frick later did during the 1892 Homestead Strike, since Carnegie was away in Scotland at the time. Does delegating this completely reduce a leader's responsibility for what a trusted subordinate does in his name, or does the choice to delegate so fully carry its own responsibility? assignments.title: Quarter 1 Capstone: A Nation Transformed, 1865 to 1898
assignments.html:
Covers: everything in modules 1 through 9, the primary sources assigned across those modules, and your own Quarter 1 capstone VR gallery.

What you're doing: one substantial piece of analytical writing, closing the quarter. Everything you have submitted so far this quarter has been a short response to a single source or a single week. This asks you to hold nine weeks together and argue something about them.

The question:

Was the transformation of the United States between Reconstruction and 1898 driven more by the choices of individual leaders, or by impersonal economic and technological forces?

You do not have to choose one side absolutely. A strong answer usually shows how both operated together in specific cases, and says plainly which one it thinks did more work, and where.

Directions:

  1. Write an analytical essay of 1,200 to 1,800 words answering the question above.

  2. Cite at least three primary sources assigned this quarter, from modules 1 through 9. Quote or closely paraphrase specific language and explain what it shows. Naming a source is not citing it.

  3. Describe and analyze at least two artifacts from your own Quarter 1 capstone VR gallery. Your weekly sticky notes are a starting point for that analysis, not the analysis itself.

  4. Structure the essay around a clear thesis, with body paragraphs organized by case rather than by week, and a conclusion that answers the question directly in light of the evidence you actually presented.

Working with a partner: if you indicated in the check-in survey that you would like to work with a classmate, you may pair up and submit one jointly authored essay of proportionally greater length. It is graded on the same rubric as an individual essay. Both names go on the file.

  4. Some contemporaries called this speech socialistic. Roosevelt asks that privilege be taken from those who have not earned it, but he never asks that private property be abolished.   2. Harlan adds that Congress's regulations of interstate commerce, "whether founded in wisdom or not, must be submitted to by all." Justice Holmes dissented in the same case, warning that "great cases, like hard cases, make bad law." What exactly was Holmes worried about, and does anything in Harlan's own sentence answer that worry?

  3. Suppose the Court had gone the other way, five to four, holding that a merger of stock ownership can never violate the Sherman Act no matter its effect on competition. Based on Week 4, how might Rockefeller's Standard Oil have been affected by that precedent, and what would have become of the 1911 case Wednesday's lesson credits to Taft?

  4. Wednesday's lesson notes that Northern Securities was in fact dissolved, and that Hill and Morgan kept effective control of both railroads anyway by holding shares in each company separately. Judge the decision by whether it solved the problem Harlan names: did it end the restraint of trade, or only the corporate form that housed it? What does your answer suggest about the limits of a court order as a tool of economic reform?

assignments.title: 14.5 Critical Questions: The Roosevelt Corollary
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Theodore Roosevelt, Annual Message to Congress, December 1904) and this week's lessons.

Directions: Answer each question in complete sentences, grounding your reasoning in the primary source and this week's lessons.

  1. The original Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warned European powers to stay out of the Western Hemisphere. Roosevelt's sentence here does something different with that same doctrine. Explain precisely what it adds, and who gains a power in 1904 that the 1823 statement never claimed.

  2. Roosevelt says the United States would exercise this "international police power" "however reluctantly." Test that word against the record in Monday's lesson: the Panamanian revolution of 1903 and the Dominican customs house in 1905. Does the evidence support reluctance, or does it suggest something else? Defend your answer with specific facts.

  3. Suppose Germany, Britain, and Italy had never blockaded Venezuela over unpaid debts in 1902. Would Roosevelt likely have found it necessary to announce a claim like this one two years later, or does the Corollary depend on that specific European precedent? Defend your answer.

  4. Roosevelt justifies intervention by pointing to "a general loosening of the ties of civilized society" rather than to any American interest. Is that an argument from national self-interest dressed in other clothing, or a genuine claim of responsibility? Judge it by the standard this course applies to regimes elsewhere: whose first-order problems, the intervening nation's or the intervened-upon nation's, does the policy actually solve?

assignments.title: 14.9 Primary Source Exercise: Gorgas on Destroying Mosquitoes
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, William C. Gorgas's A Few General Directions with Regard to Destroying Mosquitoes (1904).

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Gorgas's instructions target the mosquito's breeding cycle rather than the treatment of sick patients. Based on Wednesday's lesson, why was this narrow, specific strategy more effective across an entire construction zone than the broad sanitation the French had attempted?

  2. Gorgas explains that the larva "has to come to the surface of the water every few seconds to get air," which is exactly why a film of kerosene kills it. Carlos Finlay had proposed the mosquito theory in 1881 and was disbelieved for two decades. What does the difference between Finlay's proposal and Gorgas's instructions tell you about what a working public health measure requires beyond a correct idea?

  3. Suppose Walter Reed's team had never tested Finlay's theory in 1900, and Gorgas had arrived in Panama in 1904 carrying only the French engineers' assumptions about foul air and ordinary uncleanliness. Would the American canal effort have succeeded where the French effort failed? Defend your answer using Wednesday's lesson.

  4. Gorgas writes as though the canal's workforce were one undivided body to be protected. Wednesday's lesson records that it was not: the gold roll and silver roll system paid, housed, and fed workers differently by nationality and race, and the heaviest digging fell to the men on the silver roll. Hold both facts together honestly. Does an achievement in public health that reached everyone sit comfortably beside a wage and housing system that did not, and how should a historian weigh the two in judging the canal?

assignments.title: 15.9 Primary Source Exercise: Muir's Our National Parks
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, John Muir's Our National Parks (1901).

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Muir describes the sequoias as "superior beings new arrived from some other star," language much closer to religious awe than to Roosevelt's talk of "natural resources" and "national honor" in Tuesday's source. What does that difference in language tell you about the two different cases each man was making for protecting wild land, and are those cases actually opposed to each other?

  2. Muir published this book in 1901, two years before the camping trip. Wednesday's lesson also credits Robert Underwood Johnson's magazine campaign and Muir's letter-by-letter lobbying of California legislators. Given all three, how much of the conservation record of these years should be attributed to Roosevelt's personal experience, and how much to public opinion that was already prepared? Defend your answer.

  3. Suppose Muir had never written popular books like this one and had confined himself entirely to private lobbying of officials. Would the Sierra Club and the wider preservationist movement have had the same public influence? Defend your answer with what this week's lessons say about how the recession campaign actually succeeded.

  4. Does Muir's prose do real historical work here, or is it decoration surrounding the more substantive policy history? Before you answer, consider what Muir was trying to accomplish with a reader who had never seen a sequoia and would probably never see one.

assignments.title: 16.9 Primary Source Exercise: Bryan's Undelivered Scopes Closing Argument
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, Bryan's prepared closing argument in Tennessee v. Scopes (1925), never delivered in court.

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Bryan writes that "science is a magnificent force, but it is not a teacher of morals." That is a claim about what scientific authority does and does not cover. Is it the same claim as denying that evolution describes how living things came to be? Separate the two carefully, and say which one this passage actually argues for.

  2. Bryan never got to deliver this argument: the defense waived its own closing, and under Tennessee procedure that eliminated his chance to speak. Given what Wednesday's lesson describes about Darrow's cross-examination and the national coverage that followed it, why might the defense have judged silence more useful to its side than a final speech?

  3. Suppose Bryan had delivered this closing in open court, and the newspapers had printed it in full alongside their accounts of Darrow's cross-examination. Would the public memory of the Scopes trial likely be different today? Defend your answer using what Wednesday's lesson says about how the trial was actually reported.

  4. Bryan reaches here for the same crucifixion imagery he used in 1896 against the gold standard, now aimed at evolution instead. Does that continuity show one conviction consistently applied to new problems, or a habit of reaching for the same language whatever the subject? Explain what difference your answer makes to how you judge him as a statesman.

assignments.html:

  1. Roosevelt points to "the fate of Luxembourg and of Belgium" as a "commentary on the folly" of trusting treaties to protect the Panama Canal.   2. Roosevelt wrote this in 1915, while Wilson was campaigning toward re-election on "He kept us out of war." Both men were addressing the same question about how a nation meets an external threat. Explain why each answer follows from what each man believed about how the war in Europe had actually started.

  3. Suppose Germany had never violated Belgian neutrality, and had instead attacked France directly across their shared border. Would Roosevelt's argument here still have had the same force with American readers? Defend your answer using what Monday's lesson says about how the Belgian invasion shaped American opinion.

  4. Roosevelt calls preparedness "the prime duty of the moment," a phrase that makes military readiness a matter of duty rather than of strategy. Judge that claim by the Classical Republican standard this course applies to regimes: does a political community owe its citizens the capacity to defend itself, and if so, does that duty hold even when no attack appears likely?

assignments.title: 17.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Willy-Nicky Telegrams
assignments.html:

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Nicholas writes that he foresees being "overwhelmed by the pressure forced upon me and be forced to take extreme measures." An emperor with the authority to order war or peace is describing himself as compelled. Based on Wednesday's lesson, what exactly was doing the compelling, and was Nicholas describing his situation accurately or excusing himself in advance?

  2. Wilhelm answers that Russia could "remain a spectator of the Austro-Serbian conflict." The day before, he had written in the margin of Serbia's reply that it removed "every pretext for war." Hold those two facts together. What does the gap between what Wilhelm privately believed on July 28 and what he asked of Nicholas on July 29 tell you about how much a monarch's personal judgment could still accomplish by then?

  3. Suppose these telegrams had been exchanged three weeks earlier, in the first week of July, before Austria-Hungary's ultimatum and before any general mobilization order. Would the same two men, writing the same appeals, have had a real chance of preventing the war? Defend your answer using Wednesday's account of the mobilization timetables and Moltke's warning.

  4. Wednesday's lesson presents two accounts of the July Crisis: one in which mobilization machinery had acquired a momentum no leader could arrest, and Christopher Clark's, in which leaders retained more genuine choice than that story allows. These telegrams are evidence for both readings. Explain how, and then say which reading you find better supported by this document and why.

assignments.title: 18.9 Primary Source Exercise: Wilson's Fourteen Points
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2, Wilson's "Fourteen Points" address to Congress (January 8, 1918).

Directions: These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text above and in this week's lessons.

  1. Point XIV promises "mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike." Set that beside the Roosevelt Corollary from Week 14, which claimed for the United States an "international police power" over smaller nations in its own hemisphere. Can both commitments be held at once by the same country? Explain what "great and small alike" would actually require Wilson's own government to give up.

  2. Wilson accepted the compromises at Versailles, including the war-guilt clause and reparations his own principles had never called for, because he believed the League of Nations at the treaty's center could correct whatever else the treaty got wrong. Explain why that judgment was defensible at the time, and then explain, using Wednesday's lesson, exactly where it broke down.

  3. Suppose Wilson had not suffered his stroke in October 1919. Wednesday's lesson says a healthier Wilson might have accepted Lodge's reservations and won ratification, and also that friends and rivals alike had long described him as temperamentally unwilling to split the difference once his mind was made up. Weigh both. How much of the League's defeat in the Senate should be attributed to the illness, and how much to the man? Defend your answer.

  4. Wilson opens by demanding "absolutely open" peace processes with "no secret understandings of any kind." That proposal is aimed at a specific cause of the war. Test it against Week 17's actual sequence of events: the Kaiser's private "blank check," the alliance commitments, the mobilization timetables, the ultimatum to Serbia. Would open diplomacy have prevented the July Crisis? Say which of those causes it would have reached and which it would not.

assignments.title: Appendix A1: Yellow Journalism and the Reliability of Sources
assignments.html:
Assign any time after Week 9.

Week 9 introduced a famous claim: that William Randolph Hearst telegraphed an artist in Cuba, "You furnish the pictures, I'll furnish the war," to justify the Journal's sensationalized coverage of Spanish atrocities. Below are three things you might encounter if you searched for this quotation today.

Source 1 (a popular history website, undated): "In 1897, Hearst sent illustrator Frederic Remington to Cuba. When Remington cabled that there was no war to illustrate, Hearst famously replied, 'You furnish the pictures, I'll furnish the war.'"

Source 2 (a media historian's 2001 journal article): "No original telegram has ever been produced. The story first appears in a 1901 memoir by James Creelman, a journalist and Hearst rival, published years after the alleged event, with no corroborating document. Hearst himself denied ever sending it."

Source 3 (a 1898 New York Journal editorial, published during the war itself): "The Journal has printed nothing that responsible investigation does not support. Our critics, jealous of our circulation, invent tales to discredit honest reporting of Spanish cruelty."

Directions:

  1. Rank these three sources from most to least reliable specifically on the question of whether Hearst actually sent this telegram, and justify your ranking using at least three distinct criteria (for example: proximity in time to the event, the author's potential motive or bias, whether the claim is independently verifiable, and whether the source is itself trying to defend against criticism).

  2. Source 1 presents the quotation as simple, uncontested fact. What specific features of a website like this (or any online source) should make a careful reader pause before accepting a dramatic quotation at face value, even when it appears on many different sites?

  3. Does the fact that a claim appears in many places (many websites repeating the same Hearst quotation) make it more likely to be true? Explain why or why not, using this specific example.

  4. Choose one specific current event claim you have encountered recently online, unrelated to this course. Applying the same three criteria you used in Question 1, briefly evaluate its reliability.

assignments.title: Appendix A3: Two Immigrant Experiences: Europe and Asia
assignments.html:
Assign any time after Week 10.

Week 10 traced the New Immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. A parallel, and in important ways very different, immigration story was unfolding at the same time on the Pacific coast.

Chinese laborers, recruited heavily for railroad construction (recall Week 3's Central Pacific crews) and Western mining, faced escalating hostility as economic downturns fed fears they would depress wages for white workers. Congress responded with the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first major American law to bar immigration by name of a specific nationality, suspending virtually all Chinese labor immigration and denying Chinese immigrants already here the right to become naturalized citizens, a restriction unlike anything imposed on Ellis Island's European arrivals. The law was renewed repeatedly and not fully repealed until 1943.

Japanese immigration, arriving somewhat later, provoked a similar backlash, especially after San Francisco's school board attempted in 1906 to segregate Japanese students into a separate school. Rather than pass another exclusion law, which risked a diplomatic breach with a rising military power Japan had just proven itself to be by defeating Russia in 1905, President Roosevelt negotiated the Gentlemen's Agreement of 1907 to 1908: an informal, unwritten understanding in which Japan agreed to restrict the emigration of its own laborers to the United States, while Roosevelt persuaded San Francisco to rescind the segregation order.

Directions:

  1. European immigrants who passed inspection at Ellis Island could become naturalized citizens after a waiting period. Chinese immigrants under the Exclusion Act could not, regardless of how long they had lived in the United States. What does this specific legal difference reveal about how immigration restriction in this era was organized around more than just numbers?

  2. The Gentlemen's Agreement was informal and unwritten, achieved through diplomacy rather than legislation, unlike the Chinese Exclusion Act. What does Japan's recent military victory over Russia in 1905 suggest about why the United States handled Japanese immigration differently than Chinese immigration?

  3. Compare the push and pull factors that likely drew Chinese and Japanese immigrants to the American West with the push and pull factors Week 10 described for Southern and Eastern European immigrants arriving in Eastern cities. What is similar, and what is different?

  4. Is it historically accurate to describe this era simply as one of general American openness to immigration? Using evidence from both Week 10 and this appendix, explain why or why not.

assignments.title: Appendix A4: Florida in the Gilded Age and the Spanish-American War
assignments.html:
Assign any time after Week 9.

Florida was transformed twice during this course's timeframe, once by a railroad, and once by a war.

Henry Flagler, a co-founder of Rockefeller's Standard Oil (Week 4) who retired from the company a very wealthy man, spent much of his later life building the Florida East Coast Railway down Florida's Atlantic coast, extending it steadily south through the 1880s and 1890s. When the small settlement at the mouth of the Miami River incorporated as a city in 1896 largely because Flagler's railroad had just reached it, its citizens wanted to name the new city "Flagler" in his honor; he declined and suggested they use an older name instead, Miami. Flagler's railroad, hotels, and land development turned a stretch of Florida coastline with almost no population into the beginning of the tourist and residential economy that still defines South Florida today, a Gilded Age industrialist's fortune reshaping an entire region the way Vanderbilt's or Carnegie's reshaped New York or Pittsburgh.

Two years after Miami's founding, Tampa became the U.S. Army's primary port of embarkation for the invasion of Cuba: in May and June of 1898, tens of thousands of American troops, including Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders (Week 9), converged on Tampa's rail yards and docks, overwhelming a city never built for that scale of military logistics, before shipping out for Santiago and the campaign this course examined in Week 9.

Directions:

  1. What does Flagler's career suggest about how Gilded Age industrial fortunes, built in one region (Rockefeller's Ohio oil industry), could reshape entirely different regions once reinvested elsewhere?

  2. Why would a rail line reaching a small settlement be enough, by itself, to trigger that settlement's incorporation as a city? Connect your answer to the railroad's broader economic role described in Weeks 3 and 5.

  3. Tampa in 1898 was a small city suddenly asked to host and supply an army several times its own population. Based on what you know from Week 9 about how quickly the Spanish-American War came together, what specific logistical problems would you expect a city like Tampa to have faced?

  4. Why might a course about "United States history" reasonably still need to include state-specific case studies like Florida's, rather than relying entirely on national-level events?

assignments.title: Appendix A5: A Diverse Army: Who Fought and Who Stayed Home in World War I
assignments.html:
Assign any time after Week 18.

Week 18 followed one family's experience of the war. The two million Americans who served, and the tens of millions who did not, experienced it in very different ways depending on who they were.

The 369th Infantry Regiment, an African American unit recruited largely from Harlem and nicknamed the "Harlem Hellfighters" by the German soldiers who faced them, spent 191 consecutive days in front-line combat, longer than any other American regiment, after the U.S. Army, unwilling to let Black and white soldiers serve together, attached the unit to the French Army instead, which had no such restriction. The 369th never lost a trench and never had a man taken prisoner; the French government awarded the entire regiment the Croix de Guerre, its highest award for battlefield valor, and Private Henry Johnson became one of the first Americans of any race to receive it individually.

At the same time, thousands of American women served as military nurses and as telephone operators nicknamed "Hello Girls," operating the Army's communication lines in France although the Army did not recognize them as full veterans for decades afterward. A small number of men, conscientious objectors whose religious convictions forbade participation in war (recall Bryan's pacifism from Week 16, though he was not himself drafted), faced imprisonment and harsh treatment in military camps for refusing combat roles. At home, the same war that sent the 369th to France accelerated the Great Migration Week 11 introduced, as Northern factories, suddenly short of European immigrant labor now that immigration itself had been disrupted by the war, recruited Black Southern workers in large numbers for the first time.

Directions:

  1. Why did the U.S. Army attach the 369th Infantry to the French Army rather than deploy it alongside white American units? What does this decision, made in the name of a war for "democracy" (Wilson's own word from Week 18), reveal about the limits of that ideal at home?

  2. The 369th's combat record (191 days, no lost trenches, no prisoners taken) was, by any measure, exceptional. Why might this fact have been especially significant to Black soldiers and Black communities in America, beyond its purely military value?

  3. How does the wartime labor shortage described here connect to, and accelerate, the very beginning of the Great Migration this course introduced in Week 11?

  4. Conscientious objectors faced real punishment for refusing to fight on religious grounds. Does the Classical Republican framework this course generally uses, which asks whether a character trait serves the common good, offer a way to evaluate their choice fairly, or does it need supplementing with a different kind of moral reasoning for a case like this? Defend your answer.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains why Andrew Johnson's Reconstruction plan provoked a confrontation with Congress rather than a smooth continuation of Lincoln's approach?

answers.text: Johnson was more radical than Lincoln had been
Congress believed it had no constitutional role in setting Reconstruction policy
The Southern legislatures elected under Johnson's plan passed Black Codes that Congress viewed as recreating slavery under a new name

questions.feedback_general: Congress viewed the Black Codes as an attempt to recreate slavery under a new name, which is what triggered the escalation from Johnson's lenient plan toward direct Congressional control.

questions.text: A member of Congress who argued that the president had no special claim to set Reconstruction policy, and that the defeated Confederate states should be treated as conquered territory subject to Congress's own terms, most likely belonged to which group?

questions.feedback_general: Radical Republicans like Thaddeus Stevens argued that Congress, not the president, held constitutional authority over Reconstruction.

questions.text: The 14th Amendment's Section 2 reduces a state's representation in Congress if it denies the vote to male citizens over 21. Based on this rule alone, which kind of state stood to lose the most representation by refusing Black men the vote?

A former Confederate state with a very small Black population
Any state, since the penalty applied equally everywhere regardless of population
A former Confederate state with a large Black population

questions.feedback_general: The larger the number of adult male citizens denied the vote, the larger the required reduction in representation, so a state with a large disenfranchised Black population had the most to lose.

questions.text: Grant's presidency is remembered both for vigorous enforcement of Reconstruction through the Enforcement Acts against the Ku Klux Klan, and for major corruption scandals among his subordinates. Grant's personal reputation for honesty coexisted with a character weakness, excessive trust in subordinates, that had real political consequences for Reconstruction
Grant's personal honesty proves that no real wrongdoing occurred under his watch
Virtue and vice are only useful for judging ordinary private citizens, not presidents

questions.feedback_general: Classical Republican evaluation treats virtue and vice as character traits with real consequences, not as a single verdict of good or corrupt.

A lifetime labor contract binding workers to one employer
The trust, in which stockholders of competing firms exchanged their shares for trust certificates held by a small board of trustees

questions.text: According to the lesson, which two technologies together explain why American cities could grow both upward and outward in this period?

answers.text: Steel-frame construction and electric streetcars
The Bessemer process and the transcontinental railroad
Barbed wire and the Homestead Act
The telephone and the phonograph

questions.feedback_general: Steel-frame construction let buildings rise upward, and electric streetcars let cities spread outward into new suburbs.

questions.text: Political machines like Tammany Hall are described in the lesson as filling a specific kind of gap. Which gap?

answers.text: The gap between state and federal law enforcement
The gap between organized labor and industrial management
The gap between what formal city government could provide and what a rapidly tripled urban population, especially immigrants, actually needed day to day
The gap between rural and urban voting rights

questions.feedback_general: The lesson credits political machines with filling the gap left by city governments that could not keep pace with a tripled urban population's daily needs.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, which of the following would be the most direct evidence that American urban growth was unplanned rather than orderly?

answers.text: The spread of electric streetcars into new suburbs
The rise of Tammany Hall as a political organization
The existence of skyscrapers built with steel frames
Water, sewer, and fire systems built for a much smaller population straining under the actual population that arrived

questions.feedback_general: Skyscrapers and streetcars reflect new capability, not disorder. Overwhelmed water, sewer, and fire systems are the lesson's clearest evidence that growth outpaced planning.

questions.text: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed much of the city's commercial district, yet the lesson treats what happened afterward, not the fire itself, as the real example of contingency. What decision made after the fire mattered most to Chicago's rise as home of the skyscraper?

answers.text: The railroads' decision to bypass Chicago afterward
The city's decision to write tougher building codes that pushed builders toward steel and masonry construction
The federal government's decision to rebuild the city at public expense
Property owners' decision to abandon downtown Chicago permanently

questions.feedback_general: The fire itself did not determine the outcome. The city's choice to write tougher building codes afterward is what pushed construction toward steel and set up Chicago's later skyscrapers.

questions.text: The lesson judges Tammany Hall as having partly succeeded and fundamentally failed against a specific standard of good government. What is that standard, based on the lesson?

answers.text: Whether a political organization wins the most votes in an election
Whether a government eliminates all corruption entirely
Whether a government administers common laws regularly and predictably, so a citizen can know what to expect without needing personal connections
Whether a government provides free healthcare to every citizen

questions.feedback_general: The lesson's standard is not the absence of corruption but whether laws and access to public goods are administered predictably, rather than depending on personal loyalty to a particular man. That is exactly where Tammany Hall failed even though it met real needs.

quizzes.title: 5.7 Reading Quiz Part 2: Casson's The Romance of Steel

questions.text: Casson says Pittsburgh had "only seven small blast furnaces" thirty-five years before he wrote, producing in a year what one modern furnace could produce in eight months. What does this comparison most directly illustrate?

answers.text: That Pittsburgh's population grew faster than any other American city
That blast furnaces were becoming less efficient over time
That Carnegie personally invented the blast furnace
The enormous scale of change in production capacity brought about by the Second Industrial Revolution

questions.feedback_general: Casson's comparison is about production capacity, not population, and it illustrates just how much the Second Industrial Revolution changed what a single furnace could produce.

questions.text: Casson describes Carnegie directing "the battle from a near-by hill" rather than working the furnaces himself. What kind of leadership role does this metaphor describe?

answers.text: Strategic oversight and delegation to subordinates, similar to a general commanding a battle
Hands-on daily operation of the furnaces alongside his workers
A ceremonial role with no real decision-making authority
Direct negotiation with labor unions on the shop floor

questions.feedback_general: The battle metaphor describes strategic oversight and delegation, not hands-on daily operation.

questions.text: Casson wrote this account in 1907, describing events from the preceding decades, and clearly admired Carnegie ("an instinct" for attracting the great and rich). What should a careful reader keep in mind when using this as a historical source?

answers.text: That the account cannot be trusted at all and should be discarded
That Casson was Carnegie's business partner and had a financial stake in the account
That the author's evident admiration for Carnegie may shape which facts are included and how favorably they are framed
That the account was written before Carnegie built Carnegie Steel

questions.feedback_general: A source can still be genuinely useful while carrying the author's own bias; the skill is recognizing that bias, not discarding the source.

questions.text: Casson says that thirty-five years before he wrote, Pittsburgh had no prestige as an iron and steel centre and was "mainly an importing and distributing point." What does this detail imply about Pittsburgh's earlier economic role?

answers.text: Pittsburgh had already surpassed New York as the nation's largest city
Pittsburgh had functioned mainly as a place goods passed through, rather than a place where iron and steel were manufactured in quantity
Pittsburgh's seven blast furnaces were already the largest in the world
Pittsburgh had no rail connections to the rest of the country

questions.feedback_general: Casson's point is that Pittsburgh moved from being mainly a place goods passed through to becoming a place where iron and steel were actually produced at scale, the transformation the rest of this week's lessons describe.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what changed about invention itself in this period, beyond any single device?

answers.text: A strengthened patent system gave inventors a real financial incentive to commercialize new ideas quickly rather than keep them as private curiosities
The federal government began manufacturing all new inventions directly
Patents were abolished so that any inventor could copy any idea freely
Only large corporations were legally permitted to hold patents

questions.feedback_general: A strengthened patent system, not the abolition or nationalization of patents, gave inventors a real incentive to commercialize ideas quickly.

questions.text: What made department stores like Marshall Field's and Wanamaker's genuinely new, according to the lesson?

answers.text: They were the first stores in America to sell manufactured goods at all
They operated entirely by mail-order catalog with no physical storefront
Fixed prices, return policies, and elaborate window displays that had no real precedent in the small, personal shops of an earlier generation
They were owned and operated directly by railroad companies

questions.feedback_general: Fixed prices, return policies, and window displays, not merely selling manufactured goods, are what the lesson credits as genuinely new.

questions.text: Why does the lesson describe electric lighting as possibly the deepest change of this period?

answers.text: It completely replaced the telephone, phonograph, and patent system
It made mail-order catalogs unnecessary
It was the first invention to reach rural farm families
It meant that work, shopping, and leisure no longer had to end at sunset, making a lit city a new kind of place to live

questions.feedback_general: The lesson singles out electric lighting because it reshaped the basic rhythm of daily life around the clock, not because it replaced other inventions.

questions.text: Bell and a rival inventor, Elisha Gray, filed telephone patent papers at the same office on the same day. Based on the lesson, what actually decided that the telephone monopoly bears Bell's name rather than Gray's?

answers.text: Bell's application happened to be recorded first, a narrow and largely contingent outcome
Gray never built a working telephone
Congress awarded the patent to Bell by statute
Gray's invention used a completely different technology

questions.feedback_general: The lesson frames this as a near thing: Bell's application was simply recorded first, exactly the kind of contingent detail that could easily have gone the other way.

questions.text: The lesson closes by noting that a healthy civic culture "restrains appetite and directs it toward lawful and worthwhile ends," while advertising "by design, does the opposite." What tension is the lesson identifying here?

answers.text: That advertising was made illegal under the Sherman Antitrust Act
That a culture built on encouraging people to want more than they have may work against the same self-restraint a healthy civic culture depends on
That department stores and mail-order catalogs replaced advertising entirely
That consumers uniformly rejected advertising throughout this period

questions.feedback_general: The lesson is not condemning advertising outright. It is pointing out a real tension: an industry built to enlarge appetite sits uneasily beside a civic culture that depends partly on people restraining their own wants.

quizzes.title: 6.7 Reading Quiz Part 2: Edison's Papers and Correspondence

questions.text: Edison says he constructed "3,000 different theories" but only two "proved true" in experiment. What does this ratio suggest about how Edison actually worked, compared to a popular image of the inventor as a genius struck by sudden insight?

answers.text: A slow, systematic process of testing many wrong ideas to find a few working ones
A process dominated almost entirely by sudden flashes of inspiration
A process that relied mainly on copying the work of European inventors
A process that succeeded on the very first attempt in most cases

questions.feedback_general: Edison's own ratio (3,000 theories, two proven true) points toward slow, systematic trial and error, not sudden inspiration.

questions.text: The phrase "ninety-nine per cent perspiration" is best understood, in the context of this week's lesson, as Edison crediting his success mainly to which quality?

answers.text: Financial backing from wealthy investors
Good luck in choosing the right filament on the first attempt
Sustained, patient effort and persistence through repeated failure
Natural talent that required little effort to apply

questions.feedback_general: Edison's own words credit persistence and effort, the classical virtue of perseverance, over talent or luck.

questions.text: Edison says each of his 3,000 theories was "reasonable and apparently likely to be true," yet nearly all of them failed in testing. Why does this detail matter, based on the passage?

answers.text: Because it shows the theories were careless guesses with no reasoning behind them
Because it proves Edison worked with a large team rather than alone

questions.text: Turner first read his frontier thesis to a nearly empty room at a Chicago conference in 1893, and it became one of the most influential ideas in American historical writing only years later. Why does the lesson bother telling you that?

answers.text: Because Turner withdrew the argument after its poor reception
Because the world's fair meeting nearby proved the frontier had not actually closed
Because Turner's audience included Muir and Pinchot, who acted on it immediately
Because an idea's later influence often has little to do with how it was first received

questions.text: The lesson names real limits in Turner's thesis and then says the fact he was responding to "was entirely real." What is the distinction being drawn?

answers.text: Turner's evidence was fabricated, though his conclusion happened to be correct

His explanation told the story largely from white settlers' perspective and said little about Native peoples, Mexican American communities, or women's labor, but open land available for claiming really had run out by century's end
Turner was writing about Europe rather than the American West
Later historians proved the Census Bureau's 1890 measurement was mistaken
